sources.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case - CNBC
passages: Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.

That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."

extraction.body: Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences." Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal." "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance. A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company guilty of misleading consumers about the privacy of their data a decade ago. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew said in the order. New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said the decision could be the largest verdict by a single state against the company. "It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," he said in a press conference after the ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and ‌protect our ⁠consumers," he added. However, the company's stock has not reacted negatively to the development. Meta shares were climbing 1.77% and clocked in above $706.5 a piece at 3:01 p.m. ET. It is likely that the company will appeal the ruling so the decision doesn't have a direct impact in its finances. The case in question is related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, with the trial showing that the British consulting firm harvested data from close to 90 million Facebook users without their consent through a third-party app. New Mexico was also at the helm of a landmark case against Meta and centered on social media addiction. The company was accused of misrepresenting the impact of its platforms on the mental health of children. The company ended up settling and agreed to make several changes to its apps, including daily usage limits and "nighttime blocks" for teenagers, as well as "enhanced age assurance measures" that would prevent children from using them. Parents and guardians would have additional tools as well. According to the lawsuit, Meta "developed and refined a set of psychologically manipulative platform features designed to maximize young users' time spent on its social media platforms." New Mexico and other states pointed to features including infinite scroll, autoplay, and likes as examples of mechanisms they say encourage prolonged and compulsive use. The attorneys general also allege Meta knew its platforms could contribute to anxiety, depression and suicide among some young users but presented its products as safe.

Eight years on, Cambridge Analytica is costing Meta more than any settlement: A court in the U.S. state of New Mexico has just ordered the Facebook parent to pay a penalty of $25 billion. That is significantly more than the up to roughly $17 billion Meta agreed to pay dozens of other states in August to settle claims over its addictive platforms. At the heart of the case is the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Through a personality quiz app, data from about 87 million Facebook profiles was harvested and sold to the British political consulting firm, which used it for targeted political ads in the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign. New Mexico sued in 2021, accusing Facebook of misleading users for years about how it handled their data. Statements about its handling of misinformation and hate speech were also part of the lawsuit. In September, a jury had already found Meta liable for 43,899,725 violations of the state’s consumer protection law, according to the New Mexico Department of Justice . Prosecutors said the company made 26 misleading statements about data privacy over 11 years. Judge Francis Mathew has now set the amount of the penalty. “These communications were part of a coherent strategy designed to mislead the public,” he wrote, according to CBS News. The state had sought up to $40 billion. Until the penalty is paid, it accrues interest of 15 percent a year, according to the local newspaper The Santa Fe New Mexican. “This is a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country,” said Attorney General Raúl Torrez, adding that “no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.” At the hearing, Meta’s lawyer Matthew Nicholson called the penalty “unconstitutional,” arguing that it would drive businesses out of the state. Meta is expected to appeal. A comparison with August shows how unusual the ruling is. At the time, Meta settled in the middle of a trial in a federal court in California over addictive design and child safety on Facebook and Instagram. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences." Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal." "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Eight years on, Cambridge Analytica is costing Meta more than any settlement: A court in the U.S. state of New Mexico has just ordered the Facebook parent to pay a penalty of $25 billion. That is significantly more than the up to roughly $17 billion Meta agreed to pay dozens of other states in August to settle claims over its addictive platforms. At the heart of the case is the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Through a personality quiz app, data from about 87 million Facebook profiles was harvested and sold to the British political consulting firm, which used it for targeted political ads in the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign. New Mexico sued in 2021, accusing Facebook of misleading users for years about how it handled their data. Statements about its handling of misinformation and hate speech were also part of the lawsuit. In September, a jury had already found Meta liable for 43,899,725 violations of the state’s consumer protection law, according to the New Mexico Department of Justice . Prosecutors said the company made 26 misleading statements about data privacy over 11 years. Judge Francis Mathew has now set the amount of the penalty. “These communications were part of a coherent strategy designed to mislead the public,” he wrote, according to CBS News. The state had sought up to $40 billion. Until the penalty is paid, it accrues interest of 15 percent a year, according to the local newspaper The Santa Fe New Mexican. “This is a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country,” said Attorney General Raúl Torrez, adding that “no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.” At the hearing, Meta’s lawyer Matthew Nicholson called the penalty “unconstitutional,” arguing that it would drive businesses out of the state. Meta is expected to appeal. A comparison with August shows how unusual the ruling is. At the time, Meta settled in the middle of a trial in a federal court in California over addictive design and child safety on Facebook and Instagram. According to New York Attorney General Letitia James , who led a coalition of 51 attorneys general in total, Meta will pay at least $12.1 billion and up to $17.1 billion. New Mexico deliberately chose not to join the joint settlement and took its claims to trial instead. It is not Meta’s first defeat in the state: In an earlier trial over protecting minors from sexual predators, the company was ordered to pay nearly $1 billion there. The amount also stands out historically. Meta already paid $5 billion to the Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal, at the time the largest privacy penalty in U.S. history. The New Mexico penalty is five times as large. Mr. Torrez sees it as a warning to the entire tech industry, explicitly including social media and A.I. companies.

extraction.body: Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences." Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal." "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance. "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."

Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.

In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.

"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.

Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

The Wednesday ruling marks one of the largest-ever legal penalties for a tech giant — and just the latest court loss for Meta this year. The company, then known as Facebook, disclosed in 2018 that the private information of as many as 87 million Facebook users was improperly obtained by political analytics firm Cambridge Analytica. New Mexico sued Facebook in 2021, accusing it of mishandling state residents’ personal information and deceiving those users about its policies in connection with the incident. A jury found in September that Meta had violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act more than 43 million times. State District Court Judge Francis Mathew criticized the company for what he described as a “coherent strategy designed to mislead the public” in his Wednesday penalty decision. “Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model,” Mathew wrote. After Wednesday’s penalty decision, Meta said it will appeal the decision and has accused New Mexico’s attorney general of conflating privacy and speech issues. “This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.” Meta’s legal battles threaten to strain its business, though court penalties and settlements remain relatively small compared to the company’s earnings so far. The company reported earnings for the quarter ended in September on Wednesday, including lower quarterly profits than Wall Street had expected. It attributed the miss to a charge from the $18 billion multistate settlement it agreed to in August to resolve claims that its platforms have addicted and harmed young people. New Mexico was not a party to that settlement, which also resolved the participating states’ outstanding claims related to Cambridge Analytica. Meta posted income from operations of nearly $13 billion during the quarter, compared to nearly $23 billion that it said it would have earned without the settlement. Meta CFO Susan Li said on a call with analysts following the earnings report that the company is monitoring “active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” including additional youth-related trials set for later this year and next. Meta was also ordered to pay nearly $1 billion in a separate New Mexico case earlier this year over claims that its platforms addicted and harmed young people. Meta, along with YouTube, also lost a case in March in Los Angeles brought by a young woman with similar addiction and harm claims. Meta earnings Still, Meta’s business continues to grow at a strong clip thanks in large part to its investments in artificial intelligence. The company posted sales growth of 26% year-on-year to more than $64 billion in the quarter. Meta’s stock (META) jumped more than 3% in after-hours trading following the report on Wednesday. Meta launched its Muse AI personal assistant app in September. The app quickly rocketed to the top of app stores and has gained more than 10 million users, according to the company. It also launched its latest foundation model, Muse Wonder, last month. The company said Wednesday that its AI investments are boosting its core advertising business “through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetization.” Its average price per ad, a key metric for the company, jumped 14% year-over-year in the September quarter. Across the industry, tech companies face questions about their heavy spending on AI infrastructure. Meta’s capital expenditures during the quarter reached nearly $35 billion, up 80% from the year-ago quarter. And the company narrowed its full-year capital expenditure guidance to between $135 billion to $145 billion, the upper end of the range it had previously provided. Meta declined to provide spending guidance for next year. But investors are signaling they’re willing to give Meta some leeway, given the success of Muse, said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com. “The market has shifted from punishing Meta for spending to rewarding it for having a compelling product story,” Cohen wrote in emailed commentary.

After Wednesday’s penalty decision, Meta said it will appeal the decision and has accused New Mexico’s attorney general of conflating privacy and speech issues.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J.

We are confident we will prevail on appeal.” Meta’s legal battles threaten to strain its business, though court penalties and settlements remain relatively small compared to the company’s earnings so far.
The company reported earnings for the quarter ended in September on Wednesday, including lower quarterly profits than Wall Street had expected.
It attributed the miss to a charge from the $18 billion multistate settlement it agreed to in August to resolve claims that its platforms have addicted and harmed young people.
New Mexico was not a party to that settlement, which also resolved the participating states’ outstanding claims related to Cambridge Analytica.
Meta posted income from operations of nearly $13 billion during the quarter, compared to nearly $23 billion that it said it would have earned without the settlement.

Meta CFO Susan Li said on a call with analysts following the earnings report that the company is monitoring “active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” including additional youth-related trials set for later this year and next.
Meta was also ordered to pay nearly $1 billion in a separate New Mexico case earlier this year over claims that its platforms addicted and harmed young people.
Meta, along with YouTube, also lost a case in March in Los Angeles brought by a young woman with similar addiction and harm claims.
Meta earnings Still, Meta’s business continues to grow at a strong clip thanks in large part to its investments in artificial intelligence.
The company posted sales growth of 26% year-on-year to more than $64 billion in the quarter.
Meta’s stock (META) jumped more than 3% in after-hours trading following the report on Wednesday.
Meta launched its Muse AI personal assistant app in September.
The app quickly rocketed to the top of app stores and has gained more than 10 million users, according to the company.
It also launched its latest foundation model, Muse Wonder, last month.

The company said Wednesday that its AI investments are boosting its core advertising business “through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetization.” Its average price per ad, a key metric for the company, jumped 14% year-over-year in the September quarter.
Across the industry, tech companies face questions about their heavy spending on AI infrastructure.
Meta’s capital expenditures during the quarter reached nearly $35 billion, up 80% from the year-ago quarter.
And the company narrowed its full-year capital expenditure guidance to between $135 billion to $145 billion, the upper end of the range it had previously provided.
Meta declined to provide spending guidance for next year.
But investors are signaling they’re willing to give Meta some leeway, given the success of Muse, said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.

That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."
The tale of the Cambridge Analytica data scandal is long — and it keeps costing Meta gargantuan sums of money.
Other parts involved its data privacy policies and its efforts to mitigate misinformation on its platform.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” said C.J.
Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, in a statement shared with TechCrunch via email. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.
In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge,” he added.
Cambridge Analytica was an outgrowth of a British defense contractor, SLC Group, that specialized in influence operations and other political work.
The company notably worked with the Trump campaign during the 2016 presidential election.
It was also involved in a number of controversial initiatives .

New Mexico sued Facebook in 2021, accusing it of mishandling state residents’ personal information and deceiving those users about its policies in connection with the incident. A jury found in September that Meta had violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act more than 43 million times. State District Court Judge Francis Mathew criticized the company for what he described as a “coherent strategy designed to mislead the public” in his Wednesday penalty decision. “Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model,” Mathew wrote. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.” Meta’s legal battles threaten to strain its business, though court penalties and settlements remain relatively small compared to the company’s earnings so far. The company reported earnings for the quarter ended in September on Wednesday, including lower quarterly profits than Wall Street had expected. It attributed the miss to a charge from the $18 billion multistate settlement it agreed to in August to resolve claims that its platforms have addicted and harmed young people. New Mexico was not a party to that settlement, which also resolved the participating states’ outstanding claims related to Cambridge Analytica. Meta posted income from operations of nearly $13 billion during the quarter, compared to nearly $23 billion that it said it would have earned without the settlement. sources.title: OpenAI to bring AI models to Google's cloud, in further expansion beyond Microsoft - CNBC
passages: OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies.
Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year.
Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips.
Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42% , respectively.
All three report quarterly results next week.
OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google.
Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT.
Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.

Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems.
In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.
Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property.
The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models .
Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks.
"Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers.
That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers.

coreStoryFacts.text: OpenAI and Google have yet to confirm exactly which GPT models will be coming to Cloud and Antigravity, but it stands to reason that GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol may be included.

OpenAI says that “Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via the model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace.” This enables enterprise customers with “spend commitments” through Google Cloud to use OpenAI’s models if they choose.
Also confirmed in today’s announcement is that OpenAI models are coming to Google’s Antigravity tool, as well as Gemini Agent.

Like Cloud’s model garden, Antigravity already supports Anthropic models including Claude Opus & Sonnet 4.6 for free/Plus/trial accounts (until November 2), with Opus & Sonnet 5.5 models available to paid subscribers on Pro and higher tiers.
OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies.
Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year.
Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips.
Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42% , respectively.
All three report quarterly results next week.
OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google.
Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT.
Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.

Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems.
In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.
Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property.
The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models .

"Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers.
That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers.
Bringing GPT models to Google Cloud could be a big deal for enterprise, but even individual users could see some benefit from the deal.

Until now, Antigravity has supported Google’s Gemini as well as Claude.
Google recently rolled out Gemini 4 Argon across its AI footprint, bringing its flagship AI back to parity with the competition—at least if you ask Google.

sources.title: OpenAI to bring AI models to Google's cloud, in further expansion beyond Microsoft - CNBC
passages: OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies.
Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year.
Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips.
Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42% , respectively.
All three report quarterly results next week.
OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google.
Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT.
Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.

Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems.
In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.
Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property.
The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models .
Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks.
"Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers.
That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers.

sources.title: OpenAI's latest AI models are coming to Google Cloud and Antigravity
passages: Bringing GPT models to Google Cloud could be a big deal for enterprise, but even individual users could see some benefit from the deal.
Alongside the Cloud deployment, GPT models will appear in the Google Antigravity client.
Until now, Antigravity has supported Google’s Gemini as well as Claude.
Google recently rolled out Gemini 4 Argon across its AI footprint, bringing its flagship AI back to parity with the competition—at least if you ask Google.
It does seem like an improvement over Gemini 3.1 Pro, but it burns through tokens at an astonishing rate.
Anthropic’s Claude models are already supported in Google Cloud, but the OpenAI deal will offer another alternative to Gemini for those not feeling the Argon love.
Google says it’s now the only large cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed LLMs.
Google would certainly prefer that everyone used its Gemini models with Google Cloud services, but soon, you’ll have more options.
While OpenAI notes that Microsoft continues to be its primary cloud partner, the full suite of current GPT 6 and 6.1 models—Astra, Sol, and Luna—will launch on Google Cloud.

On Wednesday, as the company reported its third-quarter earnings, Semafor reported the company might issue non-voting stock, meaning shares that don’t give their owners a vote on company decisions, to help fund its push into artificial intelligence.

During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting. Meta’s chief financial officer, Susan Li, said the company plans to “create a new class of non-voting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders through a stock dividend.”

Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.”

The shares will allow the company to maintain its current “founder-led structure,” she added. They will also expand its “funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI.”

Meta’s earnings were strong this past quarter, beating Wall Street expectations. The company made $64 billion in revenue, a jump of 26% from a year earlier. Its costs and expenses also rose too, however, by 68% year over year.

Reality Labs, the division responsible for Meta’s AR glasses, VR headsets, and VR software, continues to lose money, though less than it used to. The company said in its earnings report that it expects the division’s losses to shrink from its 2025 levels to between $18 billion and $19 billion.

Meta has made a big push into AI over the past year. The company has released several AI models, including Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer earlier this year. In recent weeks, it added Muse Wonder and Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model whose underlying parameters are publicly available for outsiders to use and build on. Meta also launched a coding agent for software developers called Muse Code. At its Meta Connect event this year, the company announced a new line of cute and cuddly avatars for AI assistant, Meta Muse, in a push to make its AI services more relatable (and also meme-able ).

As far as can be discerned, those AI products are doing well. “In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada have set up Muse personal agents,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s earnings call. “Growth continues to be strong, and we have been number one in the App Store almost every day.”

“Now that Muse has clear product-market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it,” Zuckerberg added, claiming later that the company expects to grow the product’s appeal to eventually “serve billions of people.”

The company also noted that certain storm clouds linger on the horizon in the form of ongoing regulatory and legal issues. “We continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” said Li. “For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets, and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States.”

extraction.body: SILICON VALLEY — Meta, the operator of Facebook and Instagram, raised the lower end of its annual capital spending forecast, signaling a push to expand artificial intelligence investment. The move follows the strong reception for Muse, the AI agent it launched in September, which has bolstered the company's confidence in its AI business. To raise the money needed for the AI expansion, Meta will issue a new class of shares that carry no voting rights. Revenue in the third quarter, covering July through September, rose 26% from a year earlier to $64.6 billion, Meta said in a filing on the 21st, local time. That topped the $63.4 billion consensus estimate compiled by the London Stock Exchange Group. Meta has linked the agent to its social media services, including Facebook, Instagram and Threads, ushering in an era in which AI agents reach a mass audience. Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg said he expects revenue per Muse user to exceed the few hundred dollars a year that Meta's existing apps, including Facebook and Instagram, currently generate. He said a significant share of that revenue would come from businesses, suggesting a broad move into commerce. Zuckerberg said he expects transaction fees to generate long-term fee income but did not disclose specific plans for charging them. Meta forecast that fourth-quarter revenue would exceed the third quarter's. The company said it expects revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion for the period. The midpoint of that range is above the $73.73 billion analysts had projected, an indication that the company expects to keep beating market expectations. Meta narrowed its annual capital expenditure range to $135 billion to $145 billion, from a previous forecast of $130 billion to $145 billion, lifting the lower end. The change reflects larger-than-expected spending on data center computing infrastructure. As a result, Meta's free cash flow — the cash left after expenses are paid — deteriorated, turning negative at $2.12 billion in the third quarter. That compares with $784 million in the previous quarter and $10.63 billion a year earlier. "Our investments are paying off, our core business is strong, and we are seeing growth across the board," Zuckerberg said. Although the heavy AI spending has worsened cash flow, Meta said it would press ahead with the investment by issuing stock. The company plans to issue new non-voting Class C common shares in January 2027, a move expected to amount effectively to a two-for-one stock split. "The goal is to fund growth and help the company maintain its leading position amid intense competition at home and abroad," Meta said. "Issuing Class C common stock will help sustain the founder-led model that has driven the company's success since its founding." Investors welcomed the news that Muse's popularity was translating into earnings. Meta shares rose 0.47% in regular trading, then jumped more than 6% after the results were released, before paring the gain to 3.67% as of 5:14 p.m.

Meta shares surged more than 4% in early after-hours trading Wednesday as the Facebook parent reported a 26% jump in quarterly revenue and unveiled plans for a new class of stock that could help finance its massive artificial intelligence spending. Shares of the social media giant jumped 4% to $726 in after-hours trading as of 4:05 p.m. Wednesday, up nearly $30 from their closing price of $697.52. The rally came as Mark Zuckerberg’s company reported third-quarter revenue of $64.6 billion , up 26% from $51.2 billion a year earlier, as advertising sales climbed 26% to $63.1 billion. The Menlo Park, Calif.-based tech giant also forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion and signaled plans to continue spending aggressively on artificial intelligence next year. “Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board,” Zuckerberg said in a statement. Meta said advertising impressions across its family of apps, which includes Facebook and Instagram, rose 10% from a year earlier, while the average price per ad jumped 14%. The company reported net income of $9.86 billion, or $3.83 per diluted share, compared with $2.71 billion, or $1.05 per diluted share, in the year-earlier period. But Meta’s earnings were weighed down by a nearly $10 billion charge tied to a sweeping legal settlement. Meta booked a $9.89 billion charge tied to an August agreement with 52 state attorneys general to resolve litigation related to teen mental health and social media. The agreement calls for payments of up to about $18.59 billion. The charge helped drive a 37% decline in operating income to $12.99 billion, even as sales continued to climb. Excluding the legal charge, Meta said operating profit would have reached $22.88 billion, while diluted earnings per share would have been $7.40. The company’s bottom line also benefited from a sharply lower income tax provision of $3.14 billion, down from $18.95 billion in the year-earlier quarter. Meta also unveiled a major shake-up of its capital structure, announcing plans for a new class of non-voting shares that could help bankroll its AI ambitions while preserving Zuckerberg’s leadership of the company. The board approved the creation of publicly traded, nonvoting Class C shares, with the new structure set to take effect Jan. 19, 2027. Meta’s existing Class A shares trade on Nasdaq, while the new Class C stock will carry no voting rights. Under the plan, shareholders will receive one nonvoting Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they own, with the distribution date to be determined. Meta said the distribution is expected to have the effect of a two-for-one stock split on the market price of its Class A shares, without changing shareholders’ voting power. The announcement comes as Meta ramps up spending on artificial intelligence. Capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, totaled $34.91 billion during the third quarter. The company now expects full-year capital expenditures of between $135 billion and $145 billion, narrowing its previous forecast of $130 billion to $145 billion. The spending helped push quarterly free cash flow into negative territory, with an outflow of $2.12 billion compared with positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion a year earlier. Meta said its AI investments were already generating additional advertising revenue through improved recommendations, stronger engagement and more efficient monetization. “We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone — including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model,” Zuckerberg said. The company also plans to shift investment away from its Reality Labs division, which develops virtual- and augmented-reality products, toward AI.

During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting.

Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.”
The company made $64 billion in revenue, a jump of 26% from a year earlier.
Its costs and expenses also rose too, however, by 68% year over year.

The company has released several AI models, including Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer earlier this year.
Meta also launched a coding agent for software developers called Muse Code.

Susan Li, Meta’s chief financial officer, added during an earnings call that the new class of shares will “expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI.” Meta has poured billions of dollars into the AI race as it builds (and promotes) sprawling data centers, poaches top talent from other companies like OpenAI, and builds AI models capable of rivaling those from other tech giants.

“The scale of investment required to compete, sustain growth, expand infrastructure, and pursue new strategic initiatives amidst the AI transformation taking place in the industry is significant,” Meta says in the press release.
It’s been a busy past few weeks for Meta, which launched its AI agent, Muse, in September.
Meta also rolled out its Muse Wonder model this week.
To raise the money needed for the AI expansion, Meta will issue a new class of shares that carry no voting rights.
The company plans to issue new non-voting Class C common shares in January 2027, a move expected to amount effectively to a two-for-one stock split.
"The goal is to fund growth and help the company maintain its leading position amid intense competition at home and abroad," Meta said.
Meta shares rose 0.47% in regular trading, then jumped more than 6% after the results were released, before paring the gain to 3.67% as of 5:14 p.m.
SILICON VALLEY — Meta, the operator of Facebook and Instagram, raised the lower end of its annual capital spending forecast, signaling a push to expand artificial intelligence investment.

Meta shares surged more than 4% in early after-hours trading Wednesday as the Facebook parent reported a 26% jump in quarterly revenue and unveiled plans for a new class of stock that could help finance its massive artificial intelligence spending.
Excluding the legal charge, Meta said operating profit would have reached $22.88 billion, while diluted earnings per share would have been $7.40.
The Menlo Park, Calif.-based tech giant also forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion and signaled plans to continue spending aggressively on artificial intelligence next year.
Meta’s existing Class A shares trade on Nasdaq, while the new Class C stock will carry no voting rights.
Meta said advertising impressions across its family of apps, which includes Facebook and Instagram, rose 10% from a year earlier, while the average price per ad jumped 14%.
Meta booked a $9.89 billion charge tied to an August agreement with 52 state attorneys general to resolve litigation related to teen mental health and social media.
Meta said its AI investments were already generating additional advertising revenue through improved recommendations, stronger engagement and more efficient monetization.

On Wednesday, as the company reported its third-quarter earnings, Semafor reported the company might issue non-voting stock, meaning shares that don’t give their owners a vote on company decisions, to help fund its push into artificial intelligence. During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting. Meta’s chief financial officer, Susan Li, said the company plans to “create a new class of non-voting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders through a stock dividend.” Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.” The shares will allow the company to maintain its current “founder-led structure,” she added. They will also expand its “funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI.” Meta’s earnings were strong this past quarter, beating Wall Street expectations. The company made $64 billion in revenue, a jump of 26% from a year earlier. Its costs and expenses also rose too, however, by 68% year over year. Reality Labs, the division responsible for Meta’s AR glasses, VR headsets, and VR software, continues to lose money, though less than it used to. The company said in its earnings report that it expects the division’s losses to shrink from its 2025 levels to between $18 billion and $19 billion. Meta has made a big push into AI over the past year. The company has released several AI models, including Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer earlier this year. In recent weeks, it added Muse Wonder and Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model whose underlying parameters are publicly available for outsiders to use and build on. Meta also launched a coding agent for software developers called Muse Code. At its Meta Connect event this year, the company announced a new line of cute and cuddly avatars for AI assistant, Meta Muse, in a push to make its AI services more relatable (and also meme-able ). passages: Meta is making a big push into AI, and it’s creating a new kind of stock that could help pay for it.

On Wednesday, as the company reported its third-quarter earnings, Semafor reported the company might issue non-voting stock, meaning shares that don’t give their owners a vote on company decisions, to help fund its push into artificial intelligence.

During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting. Meta’s chief financial officer, Susan Li, said the company plans to “create a new class of non-voting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders through a stock dividend.”

Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.”

The shares will allow the company to maintain its current “founder-led structure,” she added. They will also expand its “funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI.”

Meta’s earnings were strong this past quarter, beating Wall Street expectations. The company made $64 billion in revenue, a jump of 26% from a year earlier. Its costs and expenses also rose too, however, by 68% year over year.

Reality Labs, the division responsible for Meta’s AR glasses, VR headsets, and VR software, continues to lose money, though less than it used to. The company said in its earnings report that it expects the division’s losses to shrink from its 2025 levels to between $18 billion and $19 billion.

Meta has made a big push into AI over the past year. The company has released several AI models, including Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer earlier this year. In recent weeks, it added Muse Wonder and Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model whose underlying parameters are publicly available for outsiders to use and build on. Meta also launched a coding agent for software developers called Muse Code. At its Meta Connect event this year, the company announced a new line of cute and cuddly avatars for AI assistant, Meta Muse, in a push to make its AI services more relatable (and also meme-able ).

As far as can be discerned, those AI products are doing well. “In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada have set up Muse personal agents,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s earnings call. “Growth continues to be strong, and we have been number one in the App Store almost every day.”

“Now that Muse has clear product-market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it,” Zuckerberg added, claiming later that the company expects to grow the product’s appeal to eventually “serve billions of people.”

The company also noted that certain storm clouds linger on the horizon in the form of ongoing regulatory and legal issues. “We continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” said Li. “For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets, and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States.”

extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. Meta shares surged more than 4% in early after-hours trading Wednesday as the Facebook parent reported a 26% jump in quarterly revenue and unveiled plans for a new class of stock that could help finance its massive artificial intelligence spending. Shares of the social media giant jumped 4% to $726 in after-hours trading as of 4:05 p.m. Wednesday, up nearly $30 from their closing price of $697.52. The rally came as Mark Zuckerberg’s company reported third-quarter revenue of $64.6 billion , up 26% from $51.2 billion a year earlier, as advertising sales climbed 26% to $63.1 billion. The Menlo Park, Calif.-based tech giant also forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion and signaled plans to continue spending aggressively on artificial intelligence next year. “Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board,” Zuckerberg said in a statement. Meta said advertising impressions across its family of apps, which includes Facebook and Instagram, rose 10% from a year earlier, while the average price per ad jumped 14%. The company reported net income of $9.86 billion, or $3.83 per diluted share, compared with $2.71 billion, or $1.05 per diluted share, in the year-earlier period. But Meta’s earnings were weighed down by a nearly $10 billion charge tied to a sweeping legal settlement. Meta booked a $9.89 billion charge tied to an August agreement with 52 state attorneys general to resolve litigation related to teen mental health and social media. The agreement calls for payments of up to about $18.59 billion. The charge helped drive a 37% decline in operating income to $12.99 billion, even as sales continued to climb. Excluding the legal charge, Meta said operating profit would have reached $22.88 billion, while diluted earnings per share would have been $7.40. The company’s bottom line also benefited from a sharply lower income tax provision of $3.14 billion, down from $18.95 billion in the year-earlier quarter. Meta also unveiled a major shake-up of its capital structure, announcing plans for a new class of non-voting shares that could help bankroll its AI ambitions while preserving Zuckerberg’s leadership of the company. The board approved the creation of publicly traded, nonvoting Class C shares, with the new structure set to take effect Jan. 19, 2027. Meta’s existing Class A shares trade on Nasdaq, while the new Class C stock will carry no voting rights. Under the plan, shareholders will receive one nonvoting Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they own, with the distribution date to be determined. Meta said the distribution is expected to have the effect of a two-for-one stock split on the market price of its Class A shares, without changing shareholders’ voting power. The announcement comes as Meta ramps up spending on artificial intelligence. Capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, totaled $34.91 billion during the third quarter. The company now expects full-year capital expenditures of between $135 billion and $145 billion, narrowing its previous forecast of $130 billion to $145 billion. The spending helped push quarterly free cash flow into negative territory, with an outflow of $2.12 billion compared with positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion a year earlier. Meta said its AI investments were already generating additional advertising revenue through improved recommendations, stronger engagement and more efficient monetization. “We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone — including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model,” Zuckerberg said. The company also plans to shift investment away from its Reality Labs division, which develops virtual- and augmented-reality products, toward AI.

passages: Tesla said Wednesday it will start selling its Cybercab to customers by the end of the year, even as federal regulators investigate whether the vehicle meets vehicle safety standards .
The gold-hued, autonomous two-seater lacks a steering wheel and other traditional controls.
During the company's third-quarter earnings call, Lars Moravy, vice president of engineering at Tesla, said the Cybercabs produced today are all destined for the company's own robotaxi fleet.
The company will scale as it learns about delivery, ownership, and fleet management of autonomous vehicles, Moravy added.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Tesla first floated the idea of selling the autonomous vehicle to third parties last month around its Cybercab event in Austin and even posted a form for people interested in buying robotaxis.
But it wasn't clear if Tesla would follow through, or how.

Current regulations don't accommodate vehicles without manual controls, though the Department of Transportation recently proposed removing those requirements for vehicles that are designed to be autonomously driven.
In the meantime, NHTSA said it would investigate the Cybercab to "examine the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues."
There is at least one obstacle that could throw off Tesla's Cybercab fleet plans.
The outcome of that investigation could affect whether Tesla, or anyone else, can legally operate the Cybercab.
"But, you know, the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transported as a service."

Tesla CEO Elon Musk has talked for years about building a massive fleet of low-cost robotaxis, but until recently, those plans centered on turning privately owned Tesla vehicles into self-driving taxis with a software update.
Today, Tesla owners can subscribe to Full Self-Driving (Supervised), an advanced driver-assistance system that automates many driving tasks but still requires the driver to take control.

The company continues to push out software updates to the system to improve its capabilities, but a human driver is still required to remain engaged and ready to take over — even though many videos show drivers testing the limits of that rule.
Automakers traditionally self-certify whether their vehicles comply with FMVSS rules, and Tesla did the same.

sources.title: Elon Musk Says Tesla Will Sell Cybercab to Customers for $30,000 or Less This Year - CleanTechnica
passages: When Tesla showed off its Cybercab concept vehicle in October 2024 at its “We, Robot” event, the question was when this would actually get produced.
Another question was whether it would really be sold for $30,000 or less.
After all, the Cybertruck was revealed at much lower pricing per range than it ever ended up costing — much lower .

Additionally, the Cybercab is designed for and based on Tesla being able to implement true self-driving, which Tesla is several years late on after missing its targets year after year after year after year after year after year.

So, after the event, famed tech YouTuber Marques Brownlee (aka MKBHD) said that while it was an impressive concept, he could not see the vehicle being sold to customers for under $30,000 before 2027, as Tesla was targeting.
In fact, he was so certain it wouldn’t be that he said he’d shave his head on camera if it was. (Not the biggest wager, but not something he’d apparently like to do.)

Zach is recognized globally as an electric vehicle, solar energy, and energy storage expert.
He has presented about electric vehicles and renewable energy at conferences in India, the UAE, Ukraine, Poland, Germany, the Netherlands, the USA, Canada, and Curaçao.
The updates come after Tesla posted a picture yesterday of the first Cybercab coming off the production line in its Texas factory.

passages: Tesla said today it will sell Cybercab to consumers by the end of this year, raising questions of what end users would do with a vehicle with no steering wheel and no self-driving software.
But then, in the same question, Tesla made another prediction.

And so as we start small this year and we learn about all the things Ashok mentioned about delivery and ownership and fleet management and autonomous vehicles in customer hands, we’ll continue to scale that.

Instead of the standard “end of next year” that we’ve heard every year for a decade , Tesla changed the answer to: “middle of next year.” In order words, Q2 2027.
Unless, of course, these Cybercabs get delivered with steering wheels – which most of the ones in the wild have these days anyway .
So, alright, that’s when Tesla says its cars will be able to drive themselves with nobody paying any attention.

It would be quite a big step from their current level 2 system to a level 4 or 5 system, which are the only categories that could be deemed as “unsupervised” as level 3 still includes a driver in the driver’s seat who needs to be ready to take control at any time. Musk then added on to the answer, highlighting that Cybercabs would mostly be Tesla-owned transport-as-a-service vehicles, which somewhat contradicts Tesla’s call for Cybercab fleet buyers which it put out the same day as its Cybercab launch event . This would leave a half-year where these Cybercabs, which are intended to come with no steering wheel or pedals, are completely inoperable. You couldn’t even push them into your driveway, because you’d have no steering wheel to help you do so. Unless, of course, these Cybercabs get delivered with steering wheels – which most of the ones in the wild have these days anyway . And if they did, then why not just call it a Model 2 and sell it to people for $25k, like you should have done in the first place ? passages: Tesla said today it will sell Cybercab to consumers by the end of this year, raising questions of what end users would do with a vehicle with no steering wheel and no self-driving software.
But then, in the same question, Tesla made another prediction.

And so as we start small this year and we learn about all the things Ashok mentioned about delivery and ownership and fleet management and autonomous vehicles in customer hands, we’ll continue to scale that.
That question was answered slightly differently than usual.
Instead of the standard “end of next year” that we’ve heard every year for a decade , Tesla changed the answer to: “middle of next year.” In order words, Q2 2027.
Unless, of course, these Cybercabs get delivered with steering wheels – which most of the ones in the wild have these days anyway .
So, alright, that’s when Tesla says its cars will be able to drive themselves with nobody paying any attention.

It would be quite a big step from their current level 2 system to a level 4 or 5 system, which are the only categories that could be deemed as “unsupervised” as level 3 still includes a driver in the driver’s seat who needs to be ready to take control at any time.

So, per Tesla’s statements today, it plans six months of selling a car that is usable by precisely nobody, to do precisely nothing.

extraction.body: Tesla said today it will sell Cybercab to consumers by the end of this year, raising questions of what end users would do with a vehicle with no steering wheel and no self-driving software. During Tesla’s Q3 conference call today , a question was asked about when Tesla will deliver unsupervised FSD to customer cars. That question was answered slightly differently than usual. Instead of the standard “end of next year” that we’ve heard every year for a decade , Tesla changed the answer to: “middle of next year.” In order words, Q2 2027. So, alright, that’s when Tesla says its cars will be able to drive themselves with nobody paying any attention. Great. It would be quite a big step from their current level 2 system to a level 4 or 5 system, which are the only categories that could be deemed as “unsupervised” as level 3 still includes a driver in the driver’s seat who needs to be ready to take control at any time. But then, in the same question, Tesla made another prediction. VP of Engineering Lars Moravy said that Cybercab will be in customer hands by the end of this year – which means within the next two months. Here’s the answer: In short we’re trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year in 2026, obviously we’re producing a lot in Texas but all of those are going to our own internal Robotaxi fleet, and as Tesla grows we’ll mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers and Cybercab will be the first. And so as we start small this year and we learn about all the things Ashok mentioned about delivery and ownership and fleet management and autonomous vehicles in customer hands, we’ll continue to scale that. Musk then added on to the answer, highlighting that Cybercabs would mostly be Tesla-owned transport-as-a-service vehicles, which somewhat contradicts Tesla’s call for Cybercab fleet buyers which it put out the same day as its Cybercab launch event . But did you notice anything? Moravy said that Cybercabs would be in customer hands – that is, not Tesla’s hands – by the end of 2026. And Ashok, in his answer which we reported on here, said unsupervised FSD would be in customer hands in Q2 2027 (if that’s to be believed). This would leave a half-year where these Cybercabs, which are intended to come with no steering wheel or pedals, are completely inoperable. You couldn’t even push them into your driveway, because you’d have no steering wheel to help you do so. Unless, of course, these Cybercabs get delivered with steering wheels – which most of the ones in the wild have these days anyway . And if they did, then why not just call it a Model 2 and sell it to people for $25k, like you should have done in the first place ? Either that, or the vehicles will be limited to the same areas that Cybercabs are already limited to. Despite Musk predicting that Robotaxis would cover half the US population by the end of last year , it is currently available only in small portions of 6 cities in 2 states . My interpretation is that he meant customers as in "fleet customers", not regular Joe Shmo customers. "Fleet customers" being a companies that want to own and maintain cybercars to run a self driving taxi service. If Tesla gives customers access to the same software it uses (which it has promised for a long time ), then presumably they could operate Cybercabs in the same areas. But Tesla said, in the same call, that it won’t give people access to that software, even in the areas where it’s already operating, until Q2 2027 . So, per Tesla’s statements today, it plans six months of selling a car that is usable by precisely nobody, to do precisely nothing. Either that, or all the timelines are made up. Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning , external .

"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.
