extraction.body: You need only to remember last summer’s wildfires in the United States and Canada, which fouled the air from coast to coast, to know the effects these blazes can have on the environment and human health. A new study has tabulated the toll from two decades of wildfires on air quality and human health in the continental U.S. The authors report that from 2000 to 2020, the air has worsened in the western U.S., mainly due to the increase in frequency and ferocity of wildfires causing an increase of 670 premature deaths per year in the region during that time period. Overall, the study’s authors report fires have undercut successful federal efforts to improve air quality primarily through reductions in automobile emissions. “Our air is supposed to be cleaner and cleaner due mostly to EPA regulations on emissions, but the fires have limited or erased these air-quality gains,” says Jun Wang , James E. Ashton professor and chair in the Department of Chemical and Biochemical Engineering and the lead corresponding author on the study. “In other words, all the efforts for the past 20 years by the EPA to make our air cleaner basically have been lost in fire-prone areas and downwind regions. We are losing ground.” The researchers calculated the concentration of black carbon, a fine-particle air pollutant that has been linked to respiratory and heart disease, on a kilometer-by-kilometer (0.6 miles) grid for the continental U.S. In the western U.S., the researchers report black carbon concentrations have risen 86%, on an annual basis, mostly due to wildfires. Not surprisingly, the highest premature mortality rates were in the western U.S., the region where the wildfires originated or that was most affected by smoke from wildfires in Canada. The authors say the increase of 670 premature deaths per year is a conservative estimate, as black carbon’s effects on human health are not fully understood. “Wildfires have become increasingly intensive and frequent in the western U.S., resulting in a significant increase in smoke-related emissions in populated areas,” Wang and his team write. “This has likely contributed to a decline in air quality and an increase in attributable mortality.” The fires also have affected the Midwest. Smoke transported in the atmosphere affects air quality, though direct effects on health appear, for now, to be minimal. But, Wang says, “we are on the borderline. If fires increase or become more frequent, our air quality will get worse.” The eastern U.S. had no major declines in air quality during the 2000-20 time period. The researchers derived black carbon concentrations and premature deaths estimates from satellite data and 500 ground-based stations that monitor air quality. The data from surface stations can be extensive, but it does not give complete spatial coverage and can be lacking in rural areas. So, the researchers employed “deep learning,” which enables computer systems to cluster data and produce accurate predictions, to calculate the black carbon concentrations. They calculated premature deaths through a formula that incorporated average life span, black carbon exposure, and population density. “This is the first time to look at black carbon concentrations everywhere, and at one-kilometer resolution,” Wang says. Jing Wei , the study’s lead author, led the collection of satellite data of fine particulates and the analysis of these pollutants on public health when he was a postdoctoral research scholar in Wang’s research group at Iowa. “The increasing number and intensity of wildfires in the U.S. counteract or even overshadow the reduction in anthropogenic emissions, exacerbating air pollution and heightening the risks of both morbidity and mortality,” says Wei, now assistant research scientist at the University of Maryland’s Earth System Science Interdisciplinary Center. The study, “Long-term mortality burden trends attributed to black carbon and PM2.5 from wildfire emissions across the continental US from 2000-2020: a deep learning modelling study,” was published online Dec. 4 in the journal The Lancet Planetary Health . Zhanqing Li, from the University of Maryland's Earth System Science Interdisciplinary Center, who supervises Wei, is a co-corresponding author. Contributing authors include Shobha Kondragunta, from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s STAR Center for Satellite Applications and Research; Susan Anenberg, from George Washington University; Yi Wang and Huanxin Zhang, from Iowa; David Diner, from the California Institute of Technology and NASA Jet Propulsion Lab; Jenny Hand, from Colorado State University; Alexei Lyapustin, Ralph Kahn, Peter Colarco, and Arlindo da Silva, from NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; and Charles Ichoku, from the University of Maryland-Baltimore County.

extraction.body: Celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary’s proposed $70-billion data centre, designed to run on 7.5 gigawatts of gas-fired power, could raise Alberta’s greenhouse gas emissions to levels not seen since the coal era , according to estimates obtained by The Energy Mix . Planned in an area battling drought, the project’s water needs would also be vast, rivalling the annual use of hundreds of thousands of Alberta households. Called “Wonder Valley,” the project is still nowhere near getting off the ground. But if it ever gets built as planned, it could pump out 25.7 to 30.5 megatonnes of emissions a year, depending on what turbines and gas are used, and whether or not it includes carbon capture, found Pembina Institute senior analyst Jason Wang, who crunched the numbers for The Mix . “It would be the equivalent of a return to the era of mostly coal-fired electricity,” said Wang. The reversal would set the province and Canada back about 20 years, matching the 27 megatonnes of coal emissions Alberta phased out between 2005 and 2023. The data centre complex, which O’Leary claims will be the “largest on Earth,” would require the equivalent of about 10% of all gas supply in Alberta once fully operational. It’s still just a concept, but in the Municipal District of Greenview where it’s planned, local officials are confident it will be built. “We’re about to pull off the largest project in Canadian history in this sector, and I think Greenview should be really proud of that,” chief administrative officer Stacey Wabick told council members at a budget review meeting in November. Wonder Valley was announced with great fanfare last December, a few days after the Alberta government unveiled a new data centre strategy designed to attract $100 billion in investments. At the time, Innovation Minister Nate Glubish said data centres would play a “ significant role ” in Premier Danielle Smith’s plan to double oil and gas production by increasing domestic demand for gas. The land designated for Wonder Valley is south of Grande Prairie, about 460 kilometres northwest of Edmonton. It’s located on the massive Montney Formation, one of North America’s, and perhaps one of the world’s, largest gas reservoirs. Wang said the first phase of the project, requiring 1,400 megawatts (MW) of power, would generate about 4.7 megatonnes of carbon dioxide per year using shale gas to run a combined-cycle gas turbine, the most efficient type of gas power. That would make it one of the largest industrial facilities in the province, he said. OpenAI selects Argentina for its first data centre in Latin America Carbon capture and storage has been promised for Wonder Valley, but not necessarily at start-up. Wang said a carbon pipeline would need to be built between the facility and an injection site. “With carbon-capture efficacy at about 80%, it would still mean the first phase of Wonder Valley would be 1.3 megatonnes per year of greenhouse gas emissions,” Wang said. Another requirement for data centres is the large amount of water they use for cooling. But water is also needed to run gas power plants. Even though the Grande Prairie area is known for longer, colder winters, Wang estimated that the water needed for the fully completed data centre, including both cooling and for the power plant, would be between 112 and 195 billion litres per year. That is roughly one-third to two-thirds of the total annual water consumption of all the households in Alberta. Multiple communities in the region are struggling with drought and water supply issues. Greenview itself declared an agricultural disaster due to drought this past summer, and that same day, its council approved adding more land to the purchase agreement being negotiated with O’Leary. This story is part of the Hidden Wonder Valley investigative series by The Energy Mix . It has been edited to conform with Corporate Knights style. Jody MacPherson is a freelance journalist based in Calgary. Get all our stories in one place, every Wednesday at noon EST. extraction.body: Legal AI startup Legora announced Wednesday that it raised a $550 million Series E round, valuing it at $8.8 billion. The company helps automate and assist with workflow tasks for legal professionals, as the industry moves beyond AI assistants to AI services that help them get work done. The news comes just a month after Harvey, Legora’s biggest competitor, announced a $550 million raise at a $15.5 billion valuation; back in March, Harvey also said its annual recurring revenue (ARR) was more than $ 200 million. Legora’s Series E follows the company’s April announcement of a $50 million extension of a $550 million Series D round, which valued the company at $5.6 billion. At the time, the company said its ARR had reached $100 million. That number now stands at over $200 million, the company shared on Wednesday. Investors in the latest financing include Atreides Management, which led the round, as well as Baron Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, Menlo, and other top names. The company plans to use the fresh capital to further expand across North America. Stockholm-based legal artificial intelligence startup Legora AB today announced it has raised a notable $550 million in late-stage funding at an $8.8 billion post-money valuation.
Legora provides legal AI agents as teams are beginning to move beyond simple assistants for legal work and into full-service automation that carry out multistep work.
The firm said it is expanding its geographic footprint and offering to capture this hungry market.
Founded in 2023, Legora launched its platform in October 2024.
“Legal is a sophisticated market with demanding buyers, and the bar for software is high,” said Atreides Management LP Chief Information Officer and Managing Partner Gavin Baker.

The company said the capital will support continued global expansion, including in North America, where Legora has offices in New York, Denver, Chicago, Houston, San Francisco, Toronto and Mexico City, as well as in its markets across Europe and Asia-Pacific.

Firms like Legora exist in a space where it assists with less manual production, more technology-supported workflows, greater client pressure on pricing and a premium on verification and legal judgment.

Atreides Management led the Series E round, which also brought participation from new investors Baron Capital, Capital Group, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Glade Brook Capital Partners and J.P. Morgan. Every major existing investor also participated, including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, ICONIQ, Insight Venture Partners, Redpoint Ventures, Salesforce Ventures and Sands Capital. The round follows the company’s $550 Series D round in March and brings total funding to a staggering $866 million across eight rounds. The company said it has seen a surge in annual recurring revenue from $1 million to $100 million in less than 18 months, faster than any other enterprise software company selling through a direct sales team. The next $100 million took less than six months. Current ARR stands at more than $200 million. Legora provides legal AI agents as teams are beginning to move beyond simple assistants for legal work and into full-service automation that carry out multistep work. The firm said it is expanding its geographic footprint and offering to capture this hungry market. In-house legal teams, which represented only a small fraction of Legora’s customer base a year ago, made up 40% of the company’s new customers in the third quarter. extraction.body: Legora, a startup building AI tools for law firms and corporate legal departments, just closed a $550 million Series E at an $8.8 billion valuation. The round marks one of the largest legal tech raises ever and signals that enterprise AI is moving beyond experimental pilots into mission-critical workflows where accuracy and compliance can't be negotiated. Legora just became one of the most valuable legal tech companies on the planet. The startup announced Wednesday it closed a $550 million Series E round at an $8.8 billion valuation, joining an elite club of legal AI companies betting they can fundamentally reshape how lawyers work. Associates still bill by the hour for tasks like document review and legal research that AI can now handle in minutes instead of days. Corporate legal departments, meanwhile, are drowning in compliance requirements while CFOs demand they do more with less. Legora's pitch is that its AI can handle the grunt work, freeing lawyers to focus on strategy and client relationships. Legal work doesn't allow for the kind of hallucinations that plague consumer AI chatbots. The legal AI market has exploded over the past 18 months as large language models proved they could parse complex legal language with surprising accuracy. The billable hour model that's sustained BigLaw for generations is starting to crack under pressure from clients who can see the math: why pay $800 an hour for work a machine does in seconds? Legora's $8.8 billion valuation suggests investors believe the transition is inevitable. For context, that puts the startup in the same league as established legal tech giants that took decades to build their businesses. The company is essentially being valued on the assumption it can capture a meaningful chunk of the estimated $300 billion U.S. legal services market. The funding comes as AI startups across sectors are raising massive rounds at eye-watering valuations. Several states are still debating whether AI-assisted legal work requires human attorney oversight, creating a patchwork of compliance requirements. A $550 million raise suggests Legora is preparing for aggressive expansion, likely including international markets where legal AI adoption is even earlier stage than in the U.S. It also provides runway to weather the inevitable regulatory battles and potential liability issues that come with automating high-stakes legal work. The funding environment for AI startups remains hot despite broader tech market volatility. Investors are making big bets that AI will transform knowledge work, and legal services represent one of the largest and least digitized sectors of the economy. For law firms, Legora's valuation is a wake-up call. The economics of legal services are about to shift dramatically. Legora will need to prove its AI can handle the complexity and nuance of real legal work at scale, not just in controlled demos. And it'll need to do all this while fending off well-funded competitors and tech giants eyeing the same market. Legora's massive raise is the clearest signal yet that legal AI has moved from experimental to essential. The $8.8 billion valuation reflects investor conviction that AI will fundamentally reshape legal services, but the hard work of proving the technology can handle the stakes and complexity of real legal work is just beginning. For law firms and corporate legal departments, the message is clear: the question isn't whether to adopt AI, but how quickly you can do it without compromising the quality and accuracy that clients demand.

passages: Legal tech firm Legora has raised $550m (£410m) in Series E funding at an $8.8bn valuation as it expands its footprint in the US, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region.
In just 18 months, Legora grew from $1m to $100m in annual recurring revenue (ARR), and the next $100m took less than six months, bringing ARR to more than $200m.
Speaking to City AM in December , Junestrand said the firm would ramp up its headcount in 2026, with an “aggressive” hiring plan for London.
The tech company said the funding round will also allow it to invest more heavily in its agentic operating system, Legora aOS.
“Growth only counts if the business underneath it holds up.
We have passed $200m in ARR, and we want every dollar of it to be a durable one.
That means healthy gross margins, high retention, and a cost structure that gets stronger as we scale.
This round lets us keep building that way,” said David Eckstein, chief financial officer at Legora, said.
“The opportunity in legal is enormous and we are still early.

AI is changing the role of the lawyer, with more time for judgement and advice, and it is reshaping how law firms and in-house legal teams are organised and how their work gets done,” Legora chief executive and co-founder, Max Junestrand, said.

Atreides Management led the Series E round, which also brought participation from new investors Baron Capital, Capital Group, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Glade Brook Capital Partners and J.P. Morgan. The next $100 million took less than six months. Current ARR stands at more than $200 million. Legora provides legal AI agents as teams are beginning to move beyond simple assistants for legal work and into full-service automation that carry out multistep work. The firm said it is expanding its geographic footprint and offering to capture this hungry market. In-house legal teams, which represented only a small fraction of Legora’s customer base a year ago, made up 40% of the company’s new customers in the third quarter. It now has more than 1,000 employees across 18 offices and supports more than 140,000 legal professionals at more than 2,400 leading law firms and in-house legal teams across 80 markets. AI is reshaping the legal industry. It is accelerating research and document work, changing how firms staff and price matters, and enabling corporate legal teams to handle more work internally. The central shift has moved toward the time spent on producing legal work and the judgment applied to work increasingly assisted by software. The transition is underway, but incomplete. The company said the capital will support continued global expansion, including in North America, where Legora has offices in New York, Denver, Chicago, Houston, San Francisco, Toronto and Mexico City, as well as in its markets across Europe and Asia-Pacific. Legora just became one of the most valuable legal tech companies on the planet. The startup announced Wednesday it closed a $550 million Series E round at an $8.8 billion valuation, joining an elite club of legal AI companies betting they can fundamentally reshape how lawyers work. Associates still bill by the hour for tasks like document review and legal research that AI can now handle in minutes instead of days. Corporate legal departments, meanwhile, are drowning in compliance requirements while CFOs demand they do more with less. Legora's pitch is that its AI can handle the grunt work, freeing lawyers to focus on strategy and client relationships. Legal work doesn't allow for the kind of hallucinations that plague consumer AI chatbots. The legal AI market has exploded over the past 18 months as large language models proved they could parse complex legal language with surprising accuracy. The billable hour model that's sustained BigLaw for generations is starting to crack under pressure from clients who can see the math: why pay $800 an hour for work a machine does in seconds? Legora's $8.8 billion valuation suggests investors believe the transition is inevitable. For context, that puts the startup in the same league as established legal tech giants that took decades to build their businesses. The company is essentially being valued on the assumption it can capture a meaningful chunk of the estimated $300 billion U.S. legal services market. The funding comes as AI startups across sectors are raising massive rounds at eye-watering valuations. Several states are still debating whether AI-assisted legal work requires human attorney oversight, creating a patchwork of compliance requirements. A $550 million raise suggests Legora is preparing for aggressive expansion, likely including international markets where legal AI adoption is even earlier stage than in the U.S. It also provides runway to weather the inevitable regulatory battles and potential liability issues that come with automating high-stakes legal work. The funding environment for AI startups remains hot despite broader tech market volatility. For law firms, Legora's valuation is a wake-up call. The economics of legal services are about to shift dramatically. Legora will need to prove its AI can handle the complexity and nuance of real legal work at scale, not just in controlled demos. And it'll need to do all this while fending off well-funded competitors and tech giants eyeing the same market. Legora's massive raise is the clearest signal yet that legal AI has moved from experimental to essential. The $8.8 billion valuation reflects investor conviction that AI will fundamentally reshape legal services, but the hard work of proving the technology can handle the stakes and complexity of real legal work is just beginning. For law firms and corporate legal departments, the message is clear: the question isn't whether to adopt AI, but how quickly you can do it without compromising the quality and accuracy that clients demand.

extraction.body: Tomorrow, First. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Two critical remote code execution flaws in the PHP language runtime, found by frontier AI models after a decade of manual audits failed to catch them, put 70% of the web on notice. Frontier AI models have identified two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in the PHP language runtime that remained undetected through a decade of manual security audits. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on servers running affected versions of PHP. AI-assisted analysis identified these memory-corruption flaws, which had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. Wiz Research , which combined these vulnerabilities into an exploit script dubbed “php2shell,” identified the flaws as memory-safety issues stemming from how PHP handles fatal errors during request processing. CVE-2026-109618 involves out-of-memory (OOM) corruption, where PHP interrupts a request while internal data is only partially initialized. During the subsequent cleanup process, the runtime incorrectly treats this invalid data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 involves stale global state, where request-owned internal state persists after its backing memory has been freed, allowing a subsequent request handled by the same worker to utilize the stale data before it is reset. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, marking them as critical. The flaws exploit the runtime’s trust-through-defaults pattern: the engine assumes its internal state is consistent even after an interrupted request. This pattern of implicit trust in memory management is a recurring theme in recent infrastructure vulnerabilities, similar to issues previously tracked in BeyondTrust , nine-layer , and ConnectWise . Unlike the identity-layer and supply-chain trust gaps analyzed in our prior coverage, including the synthesis in the nine-layer report, PHP2Shell represents a distinct class of failure: it sits below the application layer entirely, where the language runtime blindly trusts its own internal memory state. One brief each morning, reported by the same minds who write Forkast. Wiz Research identified these vulnerabilities using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. According to the firm, a single researcher completed in a week what would previously have taken a world-class team months of work. Writing in the Google Cloud post she co-authored with CISO Chris Betz, Raluca Ada Popa, Head of Gemini Security at Google DeepMind, said Gemini 4 Argon made “an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.” Independently, researcher Ryan Austin of Calif surfaced the same bug class while auditing PHP under OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative. Calif’s write-up of the disclosure dates the first confirmed out-of-memory fatal to August 1, days into the audit, with the first bug reported to PHP on August 11 and a working exploit confirmed by the project on August 15. Wiz Research writes that the findings “rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” and that demonstrating exploitability required “an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve” before frontier AI models lowered that barrier. According to Wiz Research, PHP powers 70% of all websites globally, meaning the vulnerabilities affect a significant portion of the internet. The flaws impact all currently supported PHP branches, including versions 5.4 through 8.5.11, as well as older end-of-life branches. Apache mod_php represents the highest risk surface, as the exploit can succeed before any application code executes. Other environments, including PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, are also at risk. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against the latest container images for WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. While Google Cloud is not itself vulnerable, the company confirmed that users running PHP on its infrastructure may be exposed. The PHP security team released patches on October 21, 2026, in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Because PHP 8.1 and older versions are end-of-life, the project provided only minimal source-backports for versions 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Administrators are advised to update immediately. For systems where immediate patching is not possible, the PHP project recommends specific mitigations: setting memory_limit to -1 to address CVE-2026-109618, and setting session.upload_progress.enabled to 0 and fatal_error_backtraces to 0 to mitigate CVE-2026-109619. While eSentire’s advisory reports unverified claims of exploit code circulating in the wild, those reports remain unconfirmed. Rapid7’s emergency threat response covers the same pair; that page returned a 403 bot wall at fetch, so it is named here rather than quoted. passages: Researchers at three different companies said Wednesday that they used AI to discover and address a set of critical bugs that could affect 70% of the internet.
The vulnerabilities were uncovered by teams at OpenAI, Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz, and another cybersecurity company, Calif.

extraction.body: Researchers at three different companies said Wednesday that they used AI to discover and address a set of critical bugs that could affect 70% of the internet. The vulnerabilities were uncovered by teams at OpenAI, Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz, and another cybersecurity company, Calif. The bugs, collectively called PHP2Shell, could allow attackers to execute code and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. AI played a crucial role in Wednesday’s discovery, allowing researchers to conduct cybersecurity work across multiple apps in just hours, the companies said. The disclosure comes after advancements in AI have raised concerns from Washington to Silicon Valley about how the technology could supercharge cyberattacks. “With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post on Wednesday. Researchers at Wiz used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, Wiz Atlas and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol during the research process. The bugs were discovered in late August but were disclosed to the public on Wednesday after PHP had a fix for it. The PHP Foundation, the organization behind the coding language PHP that is at the center of the vulnerability, has released a patch for the bugs and is urging website operators to update their systems immediately. The flaws could allow attackers to remotely execute code, disrupt services and expose customer data, according to web infrastructure provider Cloudflare, which has been working with the PHP Foundation, Calif, OpenAI and Wiz to address the issue. The National Security Agency in a social media post urged organizations using PHP to update their systems, or take them offline if they’re unable to do so. The disclosure prompted some government websites in Europe to go offline as companies updated their systems, according to Reuters. Wiz researchers say the issue is on par with the Heartbleed bug from 2014, which impacted an encryption technology estimated to be used by two-thirds of the Web. Heartbleed allowed cybercriminals to access that data that should have been protected. Like Heartbleed, the researchers at Wiz say PHP2Shell could similarly serve as a turning point in cybersecurity. While the vulnerabilities existed for years, AI made it practical to deploy them. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post. “Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

passages: With 70% of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated.
The vulnerable code had been there for more than a decade – what AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit.
With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work.
Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security.
In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet.
In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify.
We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities.
Building the exploit required chaining multiple flaws and adapting to each target’s memory layout through repeated testing and debugging.
Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours.
As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.

extraction.body: Core PHP engine flaws enable remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure across the web. Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them. PHP is a backbone of the web: it’s the programming language powering WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Wikipedia’s MediaWiki, and many others. These vulnerabilities include memory disclosure and unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it , putting every affected website in immediate risk. Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4. Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised. On October 21, 2026, PHP released the patch fixing multiple memory-safety vulnerabilities in the core engine. These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. In this post, we explain how frontier AI helped us find and fix vulnerabilities that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. The issues described below all stem from key architecture decisions, some made over a decade ago, and were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. The work grew into a cross-industry effort to protect customers, find variants, deploy detections and mitigations, and verify a patch in time for coordinated disclosure. Nearly every PHP version is affected by at least one of these issues, including releases dating back to PHP 5.4. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory. That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself. PHP is the programming language behind much of the web, powering WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. A flaw in its core engine can affect websites across this ecosystem, even when their own application code is secure. Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security. In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet. In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify. We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities. All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors. These bugs can leave a corrupted internal PHP state behind after a request ends unexpectedly. A later request or worker can reuse that stale state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption. Below you can find a table that demonstrates what type of impact was demonstrated by each of the bugs we reported to PHP. These variants have different requirements for exploitation and can lead to different types of impact. In any case, the patch provided by the PHP team fixes the issue at its core and eliminates all variants in the patched release. As AI reduces the effort needed to develop and adapt complex exploits, vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets. We're pleased to see Gemini 4 Argon help defenders bridge that gap, finding vulnerabilities and helping patch them. We also partnered with Google Cloud, Cloudflare, AWS, Microsoft, Automattic, Fastly, Akamai, Imperva, Vercel and many others to prepare customer guidance, detections and out-of-the-box mitigations for organizations that cannot update immediately. extraction.body: Tomorrow, First. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Two critical remote code execution flaws in the PHP language runtime, found by frontier AI models after a decade of manual audits failed to catch them, put 70% of the web on notice. Frontier AI models have identified two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in the PHP language runtime that remained undetected through a decade of manual security audits. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on servers running affected versions of PHP. AI-assisted analysis identified these memory-corruption flaws, which had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. Wiz Research , which combined these vulnerabilities into an exploit script dubbed “php2shell,” identified the flaws as memory-safety issues stemming from how PHP handles fatal errors during request processing. CVE-2026-109618 involves out-of-memory (OOM) corruption, where PHP interrupts a request while internal data is only partially initialized. During the subsequent cleanup process, the runtime incorrectly treats this invalid data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 involves stale global state, where request-owned internal state persists after its backing memory has been freed, allowing a subsequent request handled by the same worker to utilize the stale data before it is reset. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, marking them as critical. The flaws exploit the runtime’s trust-through-defaults pattern: the engine assumes its internal state is consistent even after an interrupted request. This pattern of implicit trust in memory management is a recurring theme in recent infrastructure vulnerabilities, similar to issues previously tracked in BeyondTrust , nine-layer , and ConnectWise . Unlike the identity-layer and supply-chain trust gaps analyzed in our prior coverage, including the synthesis in the nine-layer report, PHP2Shell represents a distinct class of failure: it sits below the application layer entirely, where the language runtime blindly trusts its own internal memory state. One brief each morning, reported by the same minds who write Forkast. Wiz Research identified these vulnerabilities using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. According to the firm, a single researcher completed in a week what would previously have taken a world-class team months of work. Writing in the Google Cloud post she co-authored with CISO Chris Betz, Raluca Ada Popa, Head of Gemini Security at Google DeepMind, said Gemini 4 Argon made “an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.” Independently, researcher Ryan Austin of Calif surfaced the same bug class while auditing PHP under OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative. Calif’s write-up of the disclosure dates the first confirmed out-of-memory fatal to August 1, days into the audit, with the first bug reported to PHP on August 11 and a working exploit confirmed by the project on August 15. Wiz Research writes that the findings “rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” and that demonstrating exploitability required “an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve” before frontier AI models lowered that barrier. According to Wiz Research, PHP powers 70% of all websites globally, meaning the vulnerabilities affect a significant portion of the internet. The flaws impact all currently supported PHP branches, including versions 5.4 through 8.5.11, as well as older end-of-life branches. Apache mod_php represents the highest risk surface, as the exploit can succeed before any application code executes. Other environments, including PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, are also at risk. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against the latest container images for WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. While Google Cloud is not itself vulnerable, the company confirmed that users running PHP on its infrastructure may be exposed. The PHP security team released patches on October 21, 2026, in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Because PHP 8.1 and older versions are end-of-life, the project provided only minimal source-backports for versions 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Administrators are advised to update immediately. For systems where immediate patching is not possible, the PHP project recommends specific mitigations: setting memory_limit to -1 to address CVE-2026-109618, and setting session.upload_progress.enabled to 0 and fatal_error_backtraces to 0 to mitigate CVE-2026-109619. While eSentire’s advisory reports unverified claims of exploit code circulating in the wild, those reports remain unconfirmed. Two critical remote code execution flaws in the PHP language runtime, found by frontier AI models after a decade of manual audits failed to catch them, put 70% of the web on notice.
Frontier AI models have identified two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in the PHP language runtime that remained undetected through a decade of manual security audits.

The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on servers running affected versions of PHP. AI-assisted analysis identified these memory-corruption flaws, which had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade.

Wiz Research , which combined these vulnerabilities into an exploit script dubbed “php2shell,” identified the flaws as memory-safety issues stemming from how PHP handles fatal errors during request processing. CVE-2026-109618 involves out-of-memory (OOM) corruption, where PHP interrupts a request while internal data is only partially initialized. During the subsequent cleanup process, the runtime incorrectly treats this invalid data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 involves stale global state, where request-owned internal state persists after its backing memory has been freed, allowing a subsequent request handled by the same worker to utilize the stale data before it is reset.

Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, marking them as critical. The flaws exploit the runtime’s trust-through-defaults pattern: the engine assumes its internal state is consistent even after an interrupted request. This pattern of implicit trust in memory management is a recurring theme in recent infrastructure vulnerabilities, similar to issues previously tracked in BeyondTrust , nine-layer , and ConnectWise . Unlike the identity-layer and supply-chain trust gaps analyzed in our prior coverage, including the synthesis in the nine-layer report, PHP2Shell represents a distinct class of failure: it sits below the application layer entirely, where the language runtime blindly trusts its own internal memory state.

Wiz Research identified these vulnerabilities using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. According to the firm, a single researcher completed in a week what would previously have taken a world-class team months of work. Writing in the Google Cloud post she co-authored with CISO Chris Betz, Raluca Ada Popa, Head of Gemini Security at Google DeepMind, said Gemini 4 Argon made “an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.”

Independently, researcher Ryan Austin of Calif surfaced the same bug class while auditing PHP under OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative. Calif’s write-up of the disclosure dates the first confirmed out-of-memory fatal to August 1, days into the audit, with the first bug reported to PHP on August 11 and a working exploit confirmed by the project on August 15.

Wiz Research writes that the findings “rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” and that demonstrating exploitability required “an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve” before frontier AI models lowered that barrier.

According to Wiz Research, PHP powers 70% of all websites globally, meaning the vulnerabilities affect a significant portion of the internet. The flaws impact all currently supported PHP branches, including versions 5.4 through 8.5.11, as well as older end-of-life branches. Apache mod_php represents the highest risk surface, as the exploit can succeed before any application code executes. Other environments, including PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, are also at risk.

Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against the latest container images for WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. While Google Cloud is not itself vulnerable, the company confirmed that users running PHP on its infrastructure may be exposed.

The PHP security team released patches on October 21, 2026, in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Because PHP 8.1 and older versions are end-of-life, the project provided only minimal source-backports for versions 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Administrators are advised to update immediately.

For systems where immediate patching is not possible, the PHP project recommends specific mitigations: setting memory_limit to -1 to address CVE-2026-109618, and setting session.upload_progress.enabled to 0 and fatal_error_backtraces to 0 to mitigate CVE-2026-109619. While eSentire’s advisory reports unverified claims of exploit code circulating in the wild, those reports remain unconfirmed. extraction.body: Researchers at three different companies said Wednesday that they used AI to discover and address a set of critical bugs that could affect 70% of the internet. The vulnerabilities were uncovered by teams at OpenAI, Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz, and another cybersecurity company, Calif. The bugs, collectively called PHP2Shell, could allow attackers to execute code and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. AI played a crucial role in Wednesday’s discovery, allowing researchers to conduct cybersecurity work across multiple apps in just hours, the companies said. The disclosure comes after advancements in AI have raised concerns from Washington to Silicon Valley about how the technology could supercharge cyberattacks. “With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post on Wednesday. Researchers at Wiz used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, Wiz Atlas and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol during the research process. The bugs were discovered in late August but were disclosed to the public on Wednesday after PHP had a fix for it. The PHP Foundation, the organization behind the coding language PHP that is at the center of the vulnerability, has released a patch for the bugs and is urging website operators to update their systems immediately. The flaws could allow attackers to remotely execute code, disrupt services and expose customer data, according to web infrastructure provider Cloudflare, which has been working with the PHP Foundation, Calif, OpenAI and Wiz to address the issue. The National Security Agency in a social media post urged organizations using PHP to update their systems, or take them offline if they’re unable to do so. The disclosure prompted some government websites in Europe to go offline as companies updated their systems, according to Reuters. Wiz researchers say the issue is on par with the Heartbleed bug from 2014, which impacted an encryption technology estimated to be used by two-thirds of the Web. Heartbleed allowed cybercriminals to access that data that should have been protected. Like Heartbleed, the researchers at Wiz say PHP2Shell could similarly serve as a turning point in cybersecurity. While the vulnerabilities existed for years, AI made it practical to deploy them. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post. “Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

extraction.body: Core PHP engine flaws enable remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure across the web. Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them. PHP is a backbone of the web: it’s the programming language powering WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Wikipedia’s MediaWiki, and many others. These vulnerabilities include memory disclosure and unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it , putting every affected website in immediate risk. Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4. Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised. On October 21, 2026, PHP released the patch fixing multiple memory-safety vulnerabilities in the core engine. These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. In this post, we explain how frontier AI helped us find and fix vulnerabilities that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. The issues described below all stem from key architecture decisions, some made over a decade ago, and were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. The work grew into a cross-industry effort to protect customers, find variants, deploy detections and mitigations, and verify a patch in time for coordinated disclosure. Nearly every PHP version is affected by at least one of these issues, including releases dating back to PHP 5.4. sources.title: Tesla says customers can add their own vehicles to the robotaxi fleet next year — will it happen?
passages: According to Tesla VP for Autonomous Driving Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla owners will be able to add their own vehicles to the company’s robotaxi fleet in the second quarter of 2027.
But even if Tesla opens up its robotaxi fleet to customer-owned vehicles, major regulatory hurdles remain.
Tesla also revealed a new Robotaxi safety website, in which the company says it has driven 3.3 million miles autonomously.
The only additional requirement is to make sure that, for example, the customer Model Y can be part of the geofences and the fleet management that Tesla has for it to be fully autonomous.
Musk also said that by 2020, a “million” Tesla robotaxis would be out on the road.
Still, Tesla’s vehicle sales were down this quarter, as revenue flatlined and profits dipped.
Tesla has a few hundred Robotaxis in Texas and Florida, some of which still have human safety monitors.
Tesla might be confident it can clear every technical and legal hurdle by Q2 2027.
It’s important to mark this deadline because it’s likely that Tesla will sail right past it.
Still, Tesla has made steady, incremental strides in the tech behind its consumer driver-assistance features.
There’s also the tension between different types of Tesla owners.
When it comes to autonomous driving and robotaxis, Musk has a pretty clear pattern: he sets bold, short-term deadlines that end up slipping by years — or never happening at all.

extraction.body: For years, Elon Musk has been making big promises to Tesla owners about unsupervised autonomous driving and the ability to add their own vehicles to the company’s robotaxi fleet. During today’s third-quarter earnings call, the company finally gave itself a deadline. According to Tesla VP for Autonomous Driving Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla owners will be able to add their own vehicles to the company’s robotaxi fleet in the second quarter of 2027. Here’s his exact quote (emphasis ours): > Like I mentioned earlier, the software for Cybercabs and Model Y is the same. And pretty soon we’ll be able to release the same software as part of the V15 release to customers. The only additional requirement is to make sure that, for example, the customer Model Y can be part of the geofences and the fleet management that Tesla has for it to be fully autonomous. We suspect somewhere around Q2 next year is when we can turn on some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the robotaxi fleet. It’s important to mark this deadline because it’s likely that Tesla will sail right past it. When it comes to autonomous driving and robotaxis, Musk has a pretty clear pattern: he sets bold, short-term deadlines that end up slipping by years — or never happening at all. Still, Tesla has made steady, incremental strides in the tech behind its consumer driver-assistance features. But the long-promised goal of “unsupervised” Full Self-Driving remains unfulfilled. In 2019, Musk stood on stage at the company’s first AI Day and vowed that customer-owned vehicles could be used as part of a “Tesla Network” of robotaxis, earning their owners passive income while driving around autonomously, looking for fares. Musk also said that by 2020, a “million” Tesla robotaxis would be out on the road. Tesla has a few hundred Robotaxis in Texas and Florida, some of which still have human safety monitors. Still, FSD growth was a bright spot in Tesla’s earnings this quarter. More people buying new Teslas in North America are choosing to add Full Self-Driving (Supervised), the company reported. Over 75 percent of new buyers picked the feature this quarter — a big jump of almost 20 percentage points compared to last quarter. Still, Tesla’s vehicle sales were down this quarter, as revenue flatlined and profits dipped. Tesla also revealed a new Robotaxi safety website, in which the company says it has driven 3.3 million miles autonomously. That’s up from 380,000 unsupervised miles driven the company reported in July. But even if Tesla opens up its robotaxi fleet to customer-owned vehicles, major regulatory hurdles remain. And in most places, it’s still illegal for individuals or outside companies to use their own self-driving cars as driverless taxis or passenger rides. There’s also the tension between different types of Tesla owners. Older Model 3 and Y vehicles without the latest full-self-driving hardware suites (or AI compute infrastructure) are constrained by hardware capability. Dedicated vehicles like the Cybercab are built specifically for driverless passenger service, whereas consumer vehicles require additional software layers to guarantee safety without human intervention. Tesla might be confident it can clear every technical and legal hurdle by Q2 2027. But history says this could easily become just another deadline that quietly slips by.

sources.title: Elon Musk says Tesla will start adding vehicles it doesn’t directly own into its robotaxi network next year - Fortune
passages: Owners of Tesla cars will be able to add their vehicles to the company’s robotaxi network sometime next year, Elon Musk said on the company’s quarterly earnings call on Wednesday, potentially allowing hundreds of thousands of customers to make money by remotely renting out their cars as self-driving cabs.

Musk noted that the Tesla team hasn’t “thought hard” about the details of adding cars that it doesn’t directly own to the robotaxi service, and was still primarily focused on safety in Austin, where it debuted operations in June with a safety driver in the passenger seat.
“We need to make sure it works when the vehicles are fully under our control,” he said.
Tesla is trying to catch up with industry leader Waymo , whose fleet of self-driving robotaxis ferry paying customers in numerous U.S. cities.
Besides the technological aspect of such a plan, it’s unclear how regulatory and liability issues might come into play.

Tesla has gradually expanded its service radius in Austin (a map shared by Tesla online last week depicts the latest robotaxi service area in a distinctly phallic shape) and Musk said the company plans to expand it further in a couple weeks time.
“I’m not sure when next year, but confidently next year.”
Jessica Mathews is a former senior writer for Fortune , where she covered transportation, defense tech, and Elon Musk’s companies.
Tesla reported that revenue in its most recent quarter fell 12% year-over-year to $22.5 billion , the EV company’s worst performance in at least a decade.

The company ascribed the decline to an ongoing slump in vehicle deliveries and falling prices (trends that were not helped by Musk’s involvement in partisan politics) as well as declining revenue from environmental credits.
Teslas have driven 7,000 autonomous miles thus far since June, he said.

Tesla is trying to catch up with industry leader Waymo , whose fleet of self-driving robotaxis ferry paying customers in numerous U.S. cities. Musk noted that the Tesla team hasn’t “thought hard” about the details of adding cars that it doesn’t directly own to the robotaxi service, and was still primarily focused on safety in Austin, where it debuted operations in June with a safety driver in the passenger seat. “We need to make sure it works when the vehicles are fully under our control,” he said. Tesla reported that revenue in its most recent quarter fell 12% year-over-year to $22.5 billion , the EV company’s worst performance in at least a decade. The company ascribed the decline to an ongoing slump in vehicle deliveries and falling prices (trends that were not helped by Musk’s involvement in partisan politics) as well as declining revenue from environmental credits. Musk has suggested that Tesla would eventually incorporate Tesla EVs owned by its customers into the broader robotaxi network for several months now, raising the idea that individuals would be able to rent out their own cars and eventually even manage their own fleets. Besides the technological aspect of such a plan, it’s unclear how regulatory and liability issues might come into play. And, as of now, Tesla still has yet to fully remove safety drivers from the vehicles that it owns and operates on its fledgling robotaxi service. For its initial Austin rollout , Tesla has had someone sitting in the passenger seat at all times. Tesla has gradually expanded its service radius in Austin (a map shared by Tesla online last week depicts the latest robotaxi service area in a distinctly phallic shape) and Musk said the company plans to expand it further in a couple weeks time. While Tesla’s robotaxi service is currently only available to invitees including social media influencers who regularly post about the company, and not the general public, Musk laid out lofty expansion plans for the robotaxi service on Wednesday’s earnings call, saying that Tesla was seeking regulatory permission to launch in the Bay Area, Nevada, Arizona, and Florida. “As soon as we get the approvals and we prove our safety, then we’ll be launching autonomous ride hailing in most of the country, and I think we’ll probably have autonomous ride hailing in probably half the population of the U.S. by the end of the year,” he said. So far, there have been no major safety episodes in Austin since the launch of the robotaxi service, Tesla’s CFO said on the call. Teslas have driven 7,000 autonomous miles thus far since June, he said. Jessica Mathews is a former senior writer for Fortune , where she covered transportation, defense tech, and Elon Musk’s companies.

sources.title: Musk says Tesla Semi self-driving is a year away, so truckers are safe - Electrek
passages: Elon Musk says Tesla expects to have self-driving working on the Tesla Semi “probably around the end of this year or early next year.”
If a year of Musk time on self-driving has historically meant closer to a decade, truck drivers are covered into the 2030s.

In the same answer, he said Tesla is focusing its self-driving work on its high-volume vehicles — Model 3, Model Y, and Cybercab — and that Semi autonomy is “taking a bit of a backseat for the next six months or so.”
These two statements sort of clash together because FSD won’t help with the shortage of truckers if you still need them inside the truck, just like FSD in consumer vehicles.
Ultimately, Musk is talking about full autonomy inside Tesla’s semi trucks.
The first Semi built on Tesla’s high-volume line at Giga Nevada rolled out in April .
We count roughly 10 self-driving and robotaxi deadlines since 2013, and every single one that has come due has been missed.
We charted his prediction record earlier this year using data from MuskOmeter, which tracks 94 public Musk predictions.
In July 2020, he was “100% confident” Tesla would solve Level 5 autonomy the next year.
“There just aren’t enough people around who want to drive trucks, which are crucial for transport throughout America,” he said.
Here’s the problem with a one-year Musk timeline on autonomy.
In 2022, Tesla scrubbed every mention of autonomy from its Semi marketing, and the read at the time was that Tesla needed drivers and fleet managers to want this truck.
The live promise right now is unsupervised FSD on customer cars in Q4 2026, which Musk repeated again in May and which we’ve gone through in detail .
Fred is the Editor in Chief and Main Writer at Electrek.
Last year it was robotaxi service for half the US population by December.

extraction.body: Elon Musk says Tesla expects to have self-driving working on the Tesla Semi “probably around the end of this year or early next year.” Going by Tesla’s record on self-driving deadlines, it is: their jobs are safe for a long time. The comment came on Tesla’s Q2 2026 earnings call on July 22, after LightShed analyst Walter Piecyk asked when Tesla would get around to autonomy for the Semi. Musk opened with the labor shortage. “There just aren’t enough people around who want to drive trucks, which are crucial for transport throughout America,” he said. Then he framed driverless trucks as a gift to the people who drive them: “making it easier on truck drivers to have a self-driving Semi is going to dramatically improve safety and comfort for truck drivers that use the Tesla Semi.” These two statements sort of clash together because FSD won’t help with the shortage of truckers if you still need them inside the truck, just like FSD in consumer vehicles. Ultimately, Musk is talking about full autonomy inside Tesla’s semi trucks. And the timeline: “We expect to get self-driving working on the Tesla Semi probably around the end of this year or early next year.” In the same answer, he said Tesla is focusing its self-driving work on its high-volume vehicles — Model 3, Model Y, and Cybercab — and that Semi autonomy is “taking a bit of a backseat for the next six months or so.” So it’s a year out, and nobody is really working on it for the next six months. Sure. Here’s the problem with a one-year Musk timeline on autonomy. We charted his prediction record earlier this year using data from MuskOmeter, which tracks 94 public Musk predictions. Eight of them were delivered on time. That’s 9%. Another 46 failed outright. Self-driving is his worst category. We count roughly 10 self-driving and robotaxi deadlines since 2013, and every single one that has come due has been missed. In October 2016, he said a Tesla would drive itself from Los Angeles to New York by the end of the following year. That was nine years ago and it still hasn’t happened. He said FSD would be “feature complete” by the end of 2019. He promised 1 million robotaxis on the road by 2020. In July 2020, he was “100% confident” Tesla would solve Level 5 autonomy the next year. Last year it was robotaxi service for half the US population by December. This January it was Europe and China approving FSD “next month.” The live promise right now is unsupervised FSD on customer cars in Q4 2026, which Musk repeated again in May and which we’ve gone through in detail . If a year of Musk time on self-driving has historically meant closer to a decade, truck drivers are covered into the 2030s. Tesla unveiled it in November 2017 with “Enhanced Autopilot” and a demo of convoy mode, where trucks follow each other autonomously down the highway. Production was promised for 2019. It slipped to 2020, then 2021, then 2022. A handful of trucks went to PepsiCo at the end of that year, and at the delivery event, Tesla didn’t mention Autopilot or self-driving once . Convoy mode quietly came off the website. The first Semi built on Tesla’s high-volume line at Giga Nevada rolled out in April . That factory is designed for 50,000 trucks a year. Tesla told investors this week that the Semi will still be “a very small percentage” of its total vehicle fleet by the end of 2026. The trucker-shortage framing is the part worth sitting with. In 2022, Tesla scrubbed every mention of autonomy from its Semi marketing, and the read at the time was that Tesla needed drivers and fleet managers to want this truck. Now the driverless version is back as a feature, and it’s being sold as safety and comfort for the driver whose seat it eliminates. The companies actually running driverless trucks don’t bother with that pitch. Aurora has been hauling freight on Texas highways with nobody in the cab, crossing 250,000 driverless miles in March and targeting more than 200 trucks this year. Speaking of ground-breaking tech: 2027 is the 10th anniversary of the Roadster II! Fingers crossed for an Anniversary Edition. Maybe it'll come with upgraded hover capabilities, a built-in time machine, and a delivery date set for 2045. As for Tesla, the company has racked up only 380,000 unsupervised miles in a year of testing unsupervised self-driving in its robotaxi service in Texas. And to limit the damage, the company has focused on a lower-speed, geo-fenced area. I think it will be a while before it feels confident enough to increase the speed and the geo-fenced area to a degree that it makes sense for the Tesla Semi. The honest read is that Semi autonomy is a line item Musk added because an analyst asked, then deprioritized in the same breath. It’s not a product timeline. It’s a mood. extraction.body: For years, Elon Musk has been making big promises to Tesla owners about unsupervised autonomous driving and the ability to add their own vehicles to the company’s robotaxi fleet. During today’s third-quarter earnings call, the company finally gave itself a deadline. According to Tesla VP for Autonomous Driving Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla owners will be able to add their own vehicles to the company’s robotaxi fleet in the second quarter of 2027. Here’s his exact quote (emphasis ours): > Like I mentioned earlier, the software for Cybercabs and Model Y is the same. And pretty soon we’ll be able to release the same software as part of the V15 release to customers. The only additional requirement is to make sure that, for example, the customer Model Y can be part of the geofences and the fleet management that Tesla has for it to be fully autonomous. We suspect somewhere around Q2 next year is when we can turn on some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the robotaxi fleet. It’s important to mark this deadline because it’s likely that Tesla will sail right past it. When it comes to autonomous driving and robotaxis, Musk has a pretty clear pattern: he sets bold, short-term deadlines that end up slipping by years — or never happening at all. Still, Tesla has made steady, incremental strides in the tech behind its consumer driver-assistance features. But the long-promised goal of “unsupervised” Full Self-Driving remains unfulfilled. In 2019, Musk stood on stage at the company’s first AI Day and vowed that customer-owned vehicles could be used as part of a “Tesla Network” of robotaxis, earning their owners passive income while driving around autonomously, looking for fares. Musk also said that by 2020, a “million” Tesla robotaxis would be out on the road. Tesla has a few hundred Robotaxis in Texas and Florida, some of which still have human safety monitors. Still, FSD growth was a bright spot in Tesla’s earnings this quarter. More people buying new Teslas in North America are choosing to add Full Self-Driving (Supervised), the company reported. Over 75 percent of new buyers picked the feature this quarter — a big jump of almost 20 percentage points compared to last quarter. Still, Tesla’s vehicle sales were down this quarter, as revenue flatlined and profits dipped. Tesla also revealed a new Robotaxi safety website, in which the company says it has driven 3.3 million miles autonomously. That’s up from 380,000 unsupervised miles driven the company reported in July. But even if Tesla opens up its robotaxi fleet to customer-owned vehicles, major regulatory hurdles remain. And in most places, it’s still illegal for individuals or outside companies to use their own self-driving cars as driverless taxis or passenger rides. There’s also the tension between different types of Tesla owners. Older Model 3 and Y vehicles without the latest full-self-driving hardware suites (or AI compute infrastructure) are constrained by hardware capability. Dedicated vehicles like the Cybercab are built specifically for driverless passenger service, whereas consumer vehicles require additional software layers to guarantee safety without human intervention. Tesla might be confident it can clear every technical and legal hurdle by Q2 2027. But history says this could easily become just another deadline that quietly slips by.

extraction.body: Elon Musk says Tesla expects to have self-driving working on the Tesla Semi “probably around the end of this year or early next year.” Going by Tesla’s record on self-driving deadlines, it is: their jobs are safe for a long time. The comment came on Tesla’s Q2 2026 earnings call on July 22, after LightShed analyst Walter Piecyk asked when Tesla would get around to autonomy for the Semi. Musk opened with the labor shortage. “There just aren’t enough people around who want to drive trucks, which are crucial for transport throughout America,” he said. Then he framed driverless trucks as a gift to the people who drive them: “making it easier on truck drivers to have a self-driving Semi is going to dramatically improve safety and comfort for truck drivers that use the Tesla Semi.” These two statements sort of clash together because FSD won’t help with the shortage of truckers if you still need them inside the truck, just like FSD in consumer vehicles. Ultimately, Musk is talking about full autonomy inside Tesla’s semi trucks. And the timeline: “We expect to get self-driving working on the Tesla Semi probably around the end of this year or early next year.” In the same answer, he said Tesla is focusing its self-driving work on its high-volume vehicles — Model 3, Model Y, and Cybercab — and that Semi autonomy is “taking a bit of a backseat for the next six months or so.” So it’s a year out, and nobody is really working on it for the next six months. Sure. Here’s the problem with a one-year Musk timeline on autonomy. We charted his prediction record earlier this year using data from MuskOmeter, which tracks 94 public Musk predictions. Eight of them were delivered on time. That’s 9%. Another 46 failed outright. Self-driving is his worst category. We count roughly 10 self-driving and robotaxi deadlines since 2013, and every single one that has come due has been missed. In October 2016, he said a Tesla would drive itself from Los Angeles to New York by the end of the following year. That was nine years ago and it still hasn’t happened. He said FSD would be “feature complete” by the end of 2019. He promised 1 million robotaxis on the road by 2020. In July 2020, he was “100% confident” Tesla would solve Level 5 autonomy the next year. Last year it was robotaxi service for half the US population by December. This January it was Europe and China approving FSD “next month.” The live promise right now is unsupervised FSD on customer cars in Q4 2026, which Musk repeated again in May and which we’ve gone through in detail . If a year of Musk time on self-driving has historically meant closer to a decade, truck drivers are covered into the 2030s. Tesla unveiled it in November 2017 with “Enhanced Autopilot” and a demo of convoy mode, where trucks follow each other autonomously down the highway. Production was promised for 2019. It slipped to 2020, then 2021, then 2022. A handful of trucks went to PepsiCo at the end of that year, and at the delivery event, Tesla didn’t mention Autopilot or self-driving once . Convoy mode quietly came off the website. The first Semi built on Tesla’s high-volume line at Giga Nevada rolled out in April . That factory is designed for 50,000 trucks a year. Tesla told investors this week that the Semi will still be “a very small percentage” of its total vehicle fleet by the end of 2026. The trucker-shortage framing is the part worth sitting with. In 2022, Tesla scrubbed every mention of autonomy from its Semi marketing, and the read at the time was that Tesla needed drivers and fleet managers to want this truck. Now the driverless version is back as a feature, and it’s being sold as safety and comfort for the driver whose seat it eliminates. The companies actually running driverless trucks don’t bother with that pitch. Aurora has been hauling freight on Texas highways with nobody in the cab, crossing 250,000 driverless miles in March and targeting more than 200 trucks this year. Speaking of ground-breaking tech: 2027 is the 10th anniversary of the Roadster II! Fingers crossed for an Anniversary Edition. Maybe it'll come with upgraded hover capabilities, a built-in time machine, and a delivery date set for 2045. As for Tesla, the company has racked up only 380,000 unsupervised miles in a year of testing unsupervised self-driving in its robotaxi service in Texas. And to limit the damage, the company has focused on a lower-speed, geo-fenced area. I think it will be a while before it feels confident enough to increase the speed and the geo-fenced area to a degree that it makes sense for the Tesla Semi. The honest read is that Semi autonomy is a line item Musk added because an analyst asked, then deprioritized in the same breath. It’s not a product timeline. It’s a mood. passages: With 70% of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated.
The vulnerable code had been there for more than a decade – what AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit.
With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work.
Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security.
In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet.
In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify.
We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities.
Building the exploit required chaining multiple flaws and adapting to each target’s memory layout through repeated testing and debugging.
Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours.
As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.
Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world.
